points: The article examines the limitations of India's disability rights system as the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (RPwD) Act completes a decade.
Mainstream discourse and administrative systems frequently equate disability with visible impairments like wheelchair use, blindness, or deafness.
The RPwD Act, 2016, expanded recognized disabilities from 7 to 21, adopting a socio-medical framework aligned with the UNCRPD.
Data from the Unique Disability ID (UDID) system as of August 2026 shows locomotor disability accounts for over half of all cards.
Newly recognized conditions like chronic neurological conditions, haemophilia, and Parkinson’s disease represent a minuscule fraction of UDID cards.
Legal recognition under the Act does not automatically guarantee entitlements, as seen with haemophilia lacking benchmark reservation benefits.
A massive gender disparity exists within the UDID registry, with women accounting for only 33.90 percent of cards compared to 66.09 percent for men.
Invisible and fluctuating disabilities, along with high social costs of disclosure for women, create profound barriers to state legibility and support.
Governance systems must expand beyond fixed, visible categories to accommodate intermittent, invisible disabilities and gendered stigmas.
sum.text:
I n mainstream discourse, disability is often treated as a monolith and equated with what is visible — a wheelchair user, as one of the co-authors of this piece is, or a deaf or blind person. Yet disability is often not visible. As one of the co-authors intimately knows, it can take the form of enervating fatigue or an inability to stand due to chronic pain on bad days. Such disability rarely finds representation in the cinematic imagination or even in the language of rights. The Rights of Persons with Disabilities (RPwD) Act, 2016, sought to challenge precisely this narrow imagination of what disability looks like. First, it shifted from a reductive, medicalised framing of disability to a socio-medical model that recognises how social barriers — not just impairments — restrict participation. Second, it significantly broadened the scope of legal protection by expanding the number of recognised disabilities from seven under the 1995 law to 21. Third, it introduced a rights-based vocabulary consistent with the United Nations Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (UNCRPD), replacing welfare-oriented terminology with enforceable guarantees of equality, dignity and full participation. To understand whether this expanded legal imagination has translated into practice, we looked at one of the key mechanisms through which the Act is operationalised: the Unique Disability ID (UDID) system. sum.text:
The annual stubble-burning season has started. In this widely dreaded practice, farmers set fire to crop residue — the thick remnants left rooted in the soil after paddy harvest — in the field. Rising labour costs, a narrow window between paddy harvest and sowing period for the next crop, and declining farm incomes have pushed farmers in several states, from Punjab to Madhya Pradesh, to treat stubble burning as routine.
This year, however, there is a silver lining amid the dark clouds of carbon that threaten the air, most noticeably in the national capital and abutting cities. It comes from process innovation and collaborative governance in Shahjahanpur, Uttar Pradesh. Shahjahanpur district was once infamous for recording the highest number of stubble-burning incidents in Uttar Pradesh.
Since 2021, such incidents have fallen by 67%. Ramji Mishra, a rural reporter who investigated this small miracle for ON AIR, our monthly bilingual webzine on air quality, travelled from village to village in the district and sent us the details, including block-level fire count data. As we checked and cross-checked the evidence, we identified three key innovations that changed the game.
First, the administration worked closely with local farmers — small and marginal, as well as well-off farmers. The district magistrate and local officials visited villages at night, when most of the stubble burning occurs, and held chaupals (village meetings). They discussed the health risks for the farmers’ own families while also listening to their concerns.

New Delhi, October 9 (IANS): The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) should go for an off-cycle 50 basis points hike sooner rather than later and widen the interest rate corridor as the world is caught in a tailspin with emerging markets at receiving end, a report said on Friday. While recent action on rate front by RBI was welcome, its effect had already been priced in by markets and thus real impact remained absent on either yields or exchange rate front, SBI Research said. It also said widening of interest rate corridor could be most effective as tested in past times of turbulence in 2013, 2020 and 2022 over which the central bank has exclusive authority by dint of regulatory prescriptions. Moreover, the central bank may change corridor width from the current 50 bps to higher levels for limited period without disturbing repo rate at 5.5 per cent. Regulation regarding change in policy corridor is clear that while MPC determines policy rate required to achieve inflation target, day-to-day liquidity management is solely in domain of RBI, the report said, highlighting RBI's report. However, the government also needs to support RBI by relooking at enhancing flows of patient capital in debt as also equities tweaking tax and capital gains structure, it said. New Delhi: With the rupee trading close to its all-time low against the US dollar, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) on Saturday announced a series of measures to support the currency, including a special facility to meet the dollar requirements of state-run oil companies. The move is aimed at reducing demand for dollars in the foreign exchange market and easing pressure on the rupee. Under the new arrangement, the RBI will directly provide dollars through designated banks to three major public sector oil companies — Indian Oil Corporation, Hindustan Petroleum Corporation and Bharat Petroleum Corporation — from October 12.
These companies require large amounts of dollars to pay for crude oil imports. By meeting their requirements separately, the RBI hopes to reduce the demand for dollars in the open market and prevent further pressure on the rupee. The central bank had introduced a similar arrangement in 2013 when the rupee came under severe pressure during the global financial market turmoil known as the 'taper tantrum'.
The RBI also tightened rules for foreign exchange derivatives, which are financial contracts used by businesses and investors to protect themselves against currency fluctuations or bet on exchange rate movements. Under the revised rules, traders will no longer be allowed to cancel and rebook certain contracts involving the rupee. However, contracts can be extended when they mature.
The RBI also reduced the limit for taking positions without proving an underlying business requirement from $100 million to $5 million. The move is intended to discourage speculative trading against the rupee. In another measure, banks handling certain foreign exchange derivative contracts involving dollar purchases exceeding $2 million will have to maintain a cash reserve equal to 20 per cent of the contract value with the RBI.
The reserve must be maintained daily until the contract ends. The RBI has also directed banks to report these reserves daily and warned against attempts to bypass the rules. The measures come amid continued pressure on the rupee from rising global oil prices, foreign investment outflows and higher interest rates overseas, which have made investments in foreign markets more attractive.

The Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Amendment Bill, 2026 was on Wednesday formally referred to a Joint Parliamentary Committee (JPC) for detailed examination following a motion moved by the government in the Lok Sabha.
Union Minister of State for Home Affairs Nityanand Rai moved the motion after the House resumed proceedings following its morning adjournment.
According to the Supplementary List of Business, the Joint Committee will comprise 31 members, including 21 from the Lok Sabha and 10 from the Rajya Sabha. The members from the two Houses will be nominated by the Lok Sabha Speaker and Rajya Sabha Chairman, respectively.
The committee has been tasked with conducting an in-depth examination of the provisions of the Bill and submitting its report to Parliament by the last day of the first week of the Winter Session 2026. The quorum for the committee’s sittings will be one-third of its total membership.
The motion also recommended that the Rajya Sabha join the Joint Committee and communicate the names of its members to the Lok Sabha.

The Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act (FCRA) regulates the acceptance and utilisation of foreign contributions by individuals, associations and organisations in India. It seeks to ensure that foreign contributions are used for the purposes for which they are received.
The Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Amendment Bill, 2026, was introduced in the Lok Sabha on March 25 and is currently under consideration by Parliament. The revised FCRA Rules, 2026, were notified on June 22 and are in force.

sum.text:
Canada will send nearly 300 business delegates to India next week in its biggest trade mission to the country in more than 30 years, as it looks to expand commercial ties and "more than double bilateral trade" by 2030. The delegation, led by Canadian Minister of International Trade Maninder Sidhu, will visit Mumbai and Bengaluru from October 12 to 17, according to an official statement issued on Friday. The visit comes as India and Canada work to conclude negotiations for a Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (CEPA) by the end of this year.
Sidhu said, "By matching Canadian expertise in sectors like aerospace, agri-food and clean technology with India's growing demand, we will diversify our trade and attract new investment." According to the statement, the mission is aimed at helping Canadian businesses connect with Indian decision-makers, industry leaders and potential customers, while building partnerships expected to generate employment in Canada. The fifth round of CEPA negotiations was held in Ottawa from October 5 to 9. Sidhu had also met Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal on the sidelines of the G20 Trade Ministers' Meeting in Milwaukee in the US on October 1, where they discussed progress in the talks and efforts to deepen bilateral trade and investment ties.
India and Canada had announced a renewed push for a comprehensive trade agreement during Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney's visit to India in March, setting a target of raising two-way trade to CAD 70 billion, or about Rs 4.75 lakh crore, by 2030. In 2025, bilateral trade in goods and services totalled CAD 30.4 billion, according to Canadian government data. Canada's merchandise exports to India stood at CAD 3.9 billion, led by vegetables, mineral fuels and oils, and wood pulp.
Its merchandise imports from India were CAD 9.7 billion, mainly precious stones and metals, machinery and pharmaceutical products. The statement said Canada is also looking to diversify its exports beyond the United States, with India a key part of that strategy. It added that the Canadian Indo-Pacific Strategy, launched in 2022, identifies trade, security, sustainability, people-to-people ties and regional engagement as its five strategic objectives.
Overall, the upcoming mission underlines Canada's effort to deepen trade and investment ties with India, support progress on the CEPA talks and push towards the 2030 target for bilateral trade.
